extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and journalists interested in news production and gender bias
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the criteria by which journalists and news organizations decide what is news (placement, sourcing, deadlines, display) with attention to how these practices shape coverage of social movements, especially the women's movement. Useful for analyzing newsroom selection, framing, and institutional effects on topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional ideology privileging male concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional ideology to which 'newsmen' subscribe identifies male concerns as the important news stories, and accordingly relegates topics traditionally characterized as 'female' to a peripheral status as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why topics like power, politics, and stratification (male concerns) are treated as 'first-page' matters; cites Bernard (1973) and Dorothy E. Smith to argue that dominant newsroom ideologies are male and thus shape what is noticed as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft consciousness: events over issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The craft consciousness of newswork identifies events, not issues, as the stuff and substance of hard news. Hard-news stories about occurrences take precedence both in evaluation as newsworthy and in internal newsroom processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This norm privileges observable, discrete occurrences (speeches, campaigns, voting) over diffuse processes (consciousness-raising), making issue-focused, non-event activity hard to cover within standard reportorial forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable-event requirement for newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors require observable, reportable occurrences (events) that can be held to symbolize progress, purposes, or problems of institutions; non-observable political change is easily dismissed as 'not newsworthy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciousness-raising struggles—changes 'in people's heads'—lack the observable pegs reporters need (quotable speeches, named spokespersons) and therefore are often excluded or minimized in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for identifiable spokespersons/representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Newswork privileges stories that can point to a named spokesperson or representative; leaderless or decentralized movements lack a single authoritative voice and are therefore difficult to cover as coherent topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because representativeness cannot be quantitatively determined for many grassroots groups, reporters prefer identifiable leaders; absence of an elected spokesperson undermines the ability to 'nail down' what a movement represents.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Firsts' sourcing practice (use of accomplished exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often locate sources by interviewing 'firsts' (the first woman to head X) or highly accomplished women and ask their opinions about movement issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sources tend to view themselves as exceptional and often express moderate approval of movement aims, thereby producing reformist rather than radical portrayals; example: interviews with women who achieved status by 'doing' rather than 'being.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaction-story framing
rubrics_metrics.description: When editors judge an occurrence unusually newsworthy, reporters solicit the 'reactions' of public figures; reaction stories introduce controlled conflict and controversy and can import issuelike elements into coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reactions of quasi-legitimated leaders imposes structure on leaderless movements and can transform radical activity into a form more accessible to traditional news narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on routine institutional sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters routinely rely on institutional sources who are centrally positioned to know what is going on; these routine sources are often the powerful actors being criticized and are willing to disparage challengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turning to routine sources legitimates institutional power and tends to marginalize disruptive actors who lack ongoing access (beats) or who distrust the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat reporting and institutionalization as coverage enablers
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutionalized movements with offices, regular hours, and administrative structures fit the beat-reporting model and thus are more easily and routinely covered by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include ERA coalitions and the National Women's Political Caucus having offices that enable predictable contact patterns; reporters can create a 'beat' when sources are routinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadline and scheduling constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom scheduling (late-morning-to-evening reporting cycles, early filing for editions, early weekend deadlines) conflicts with many movement activities (evening meetings, weekend conferences), making coverage difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat reporters on morning papers may miss or only partially cover weekend/night meetings; movement scheduling often clashes with reporters' availability and filing times, disadvantaging coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/consumer-product logic shaping coverage priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publishers allocate provisions (staffing, budgets) based on the perceived economic value of coverage to the newspaper as a consumer product; items judged of clear economic value (sports, cultural reviews) receive resources before movement stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expensive special provisions (stringers, late-night staffing) are justified only when expected coverage is vital to product sales; women's movement coverage often judged lower priority economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of women’s pages / lifestyle sections as movement resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Segregated sections (women's page, family/style, lifestyle) that handle mostly 'soft' news can be geared to cover women's movement stories: they can ignore late deadlines, hold stories, provide longer copy, and give better display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although labeled 'soft-news,' these pages can offer more space, pictures, and sensitive editing; editors of such pages can choose to make movement coverage a priority even without managerial sign-off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territoriality and bureaucratic control over story placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom territoriality—department heads' budgets and discrete responsibilities—determines which desks cover which aspects of a phenomenon; placement choices constitute the topic and influence how a story is treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial bargaining and budget charging (e.g., foreign desk travel budgets) influence whether coverage is considered 'foreign' or 'women's page' material; territorial norms can reassign hard-news to soft-news preserves or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication site and display shape topic constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The site of publication (page one vs. women's page), length, layout, and pictures help constitute an occurrence as a particular topic and produce different stock narratives and plots about the same event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement affects what aspects are noticed and how they are treated—e.g., same conference covered tersely by a UN correspondent vs. a women’s-page reporter who analyzes speeches and interactions at length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional neutrality norms and demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters (including feminist reporters) are expected to demonstrate objectivity and acceptance of 'the web of facticity'—for example, by asking hostile or neutral questions to avoid appearing partisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists may ask adversarial questions of movement actors to prove neutrality; this professional performance shapes the line of questioning and the public presentation of a movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-aligned questioning shapes discovered facts and narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters tend over time to adopt the outlook of the news sources with whom they are associated; the questions they ask guide what they find and thus reconstitute both the topic and the world it inhabits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because questions contain their own answers, reporters' habitual source networks influence the scope, interpretation, and narratives that emerge in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization redirects movement toward routinized beats
rubrics_metrics.description: As social movements institutionalize and create centralized offices, their activities shift toward lobbying, legislation, and routinized interactions that make them coverable by specialized beats (education, courts, labor), reducing radical potential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once activities are turned into law-centered or bureaucratic routines, coverage is reassigned to non-women's beats, integrating the movement into standard news routines and possibly narrowing its portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reclassification between hard and soft news via editorial placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A story's classification as hard or soft news can change depending on which desk claims it; once an item becomes part of a 'soft-news' preserve (women's page), it may be reconstituted as soft even if it concerns hard-news subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may move stories between desks (e.g., offer a national editor's item to women's page for space reasons), and such moves influence length, display, and perceived importance.
